concerns.text: The hypothesis language "higher adolescent exposure predicts more vivid autobiographical memories" implies causation, but the design is purely observational (no manipulation or instrumental variable). This creates a causal claim that the data cannot support.

The primary predictor is a ratio (listens_adolescence / total_listens) but the model does not include total_listens as a covariate. Because the ratio is mathematically dependent on total_listens, omitted‑variable bias can confound the effect of adolescent exposure.

concerns.location: FR-001 (definition of adolescence) and Constitution VII
concerns.text: Adolescence is described only as "birth year to roughly the mid‑teens" without an explicit age range or literature citation, violating the constitution’s requirement for a precise, cited developmental window.

The analysis is validated solely on simulated AMT data where the effect size (β = 0.3) is pre‑embedded. This does not provide independent empirical evidence for the real‑world relationship and makes the validation circular to the hypothesis.

Sensitivity analysis re‑fits the model across five Levenshtein thresholds but does not adjust for multiple comparisons, risking inflated Type I error when interpreting stability of the exposure effect.
The block‑permutation test reports a one‑sided p‑value (proportion of null coefficients ≥ observed) without specifying a two‑sided test or correction, which can bias significance assessment.

The plan lacks a power analysis or justification for the chosen sample size, and does not account for observation loss due to filtering (FR‑009, EC‑002), leaving the study at risk of being under‑powered.
